About

I'm a London-based, people-centric operations professional with nine years across the digital ecosystem. I started in digital advertising, analysing search and audience data for global clients. I moved into workforce development, designing a tech sales curriculum for first-generation graduates at COOP Careers. Today I steward employment infrastructure across 20+ geographies for a distributed, remote-first organisation.

The thread through all of it is translation. In operations, I turn complex processes into human-centred systems: governance frameworks, knowledge management and practical guidance for adopting AI responsibly, balancing innovation, intellectual stewardship and organisational risk. In learning design, I turn complex ideas, from sales methodology to data and algorithmic fairness, into programs people can actually use.

Years of watching algorithms sort people into "affinity" buckets they never see shaped why I do this. I hold an MA in AI, Data & Communication from the University of Westminster, where I focused on algorithmic bias and digital regulation. I want the systems that shape people's lives to be transparent, consistent and understandable to the people inside them.

Next: COOP tech sales curriculum

COOP Careers, 2020–2021

A tech sales track for first-generation graduates

I designed COOP's tech sales curriculum from scratch in six weeks: a 17-week evening program that took underrepresented graduates from "what is an SDR?" to running mock discovery calls and pitching a client project to industry judges.

Organisation
COOP Careers (US nonprofit)
Format
Live evenings, cohort-based
Length
17 weeks, 32 sessions
Placement
64%, first cohort

Who it was for

COOP supports first-generation college graduates from underrepresented backgrounds, who learn in peer cohorts led by program alumni ("Captains"). Each cohort had four Captains, including at least one senior Captain, so facilitator materials mattered as much as learner materials.

The problem

COOP already ran digital marketing and data analytics tracks. Tech sales was an obvious next door to open: entry-level SDR and BDR roles are in high demand, pay well and don't require a technical degree. But the field is hard to read from the outside. Its vocabulary is opaque, its job titles are inconsistent, and many roles marketed as "tech sales" are really ad sales.

Graduates also arrived with a fair amount of suspicion about sales itself. The curriculum had to build skills and reframe what the job is.

"Sales is a noble pursuit if practiced nobly."

What I built

Seven modules, each made of two or three lessons. Every lesson ran about 2.5 hours, split between teaching and an applied assignment. I designed the track and wrote the core materials, working alongside sales practitioners who led individual modules.

  1. IntroductionsWhat sales is, COOP's philosophy of sales, and the B2B tech sales career track from SDR to CRO
  2. Discovering the path to the closeResearching accounts with an ideal customer profile, and structuring discovery and qualification calls
  3. Communicating valueGetting up to speed on a product, mapping the competitive landscape, and the five-minute demo
  4. Emotional resilienceHandling "no", multi-threading accounts and objection handling
  5. CommunicationCold emails, voicemails, flipping a cold call, and partnering with an account executive
  6. Technical skillsSalesforce fundamentals, email cadences and social selling on LinkedIn Sales Navigator
  7. Client project and interviewsA capstone (research a client, plan outreach, write the email, record a five-minute demo) judged by industry professionals

Supporting materials included a self-study primer on the industry and its terminology, slide decks for each module, and a mock cold-calling open house.

Design approach

  • Demystify first. Name the jargon (SaaS, CRM, BANT, pipeline) and give people simple tests, like "do you sell software?", for reading job descriptions honestly.
  • Practise more than you lecture. The open house put four COOPers in each of eight breakout rooms, running timed five-minute calls through small-, mid- and enterprise-account scenarios with volunteer practitioners.
  • Make it real. Scenarios used recognisable accounts and genuine friction: gatekeepers, a lead who left the company three years ago, a competitor already in place.
  • Build interview readiness in. Lessons were mapped directly to the questions hiring managers ask, so learners left each session with answers, not only notes.

Outcomes

64%job placement rate for the first cohort, across digital and programmatic roles
  • Measured what mattered. I designed the monitoring and evaluation framework used to track the first cohort through to placement.
  • Standardised the curriculum. I built programmatic training decks and workshops (SEM, The Trade Desk, display) that became the standard for future cohorts.
  • Widened the door. I launched the Women in Tech Sales Empowerment Panel and developed equity-focused initiatives that were adopted nationally.

COOP tech sales alumni went on to roles at companies including:

  • Snowflake
  • DocuSign
  • HubSpot
  • Workday
  • Plaid
  • New Relic
  • Zuora
  • Darktrace
  • Sezzle
  • airSlate
  • Augmedix
  • JobScore

Next: Data literacy nano-learning

Data literacy teaching sample, 2025

When does a project need a privacy check?

A 30-minute nano-learning that introduces AI and ethics through one practical question: how do you tell when a project could put people's data at high risk, and needs a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)?

Format
Nano-learning, live
Length
30 minutes
Audience
50+ learners
Topic
Intro to AI and ethics

Audience

Learners of all ages and backgrounds meeting AI and ethics for the first time. Most would never write a line of code, but all of them use, buy or are judged by data-driven products. The session had to work without legal or technical vocabulary, and still leave people with something they could apply to a real system.

Structure

  1. Set the goalOne outcome for the session: recognise when a project needs a DPIA.
  2. Anchor it in the lawArticle 35(1) of the GDPR, read together and translated into plain language.
  3. Give it a pictureA DPIA trigger is like a warning light on your car's dashboard: it doesn't mean the engine has failed, it means stop and check.
  4. Hand over a rule of thumbThe European Data Protection Board's checklist of risk signs: one sign, keep an eye on it; two or more, a DPIA is strongly suggested.
  5. Walk a real caseHireVue's AI video interviews, tested against four triggers: sensitive data, new technology, large-scale processing, and profiling or automated decisions.
  6. Recap and connectThree takeaways, linked to the EU AI Act's tiers of risk.
  7. Apply itA hands-on scenario and a multiple-choice check, where learners justify a decision using the triggers.

We don't DPIA everything. We learn to spot the warning lights.

Design approach

  • One question, answered well. In 30 minutes, depth beats coverage. Everything in the session serves a single decision learners can make on their own afterwards.
  • Metaphor before mechanism. The dashboard warning light gives non-specialists a mental model before they meet the regulatory language.
  • A real system, not a hypothetical. Hiring is something everyone has experienced, so an AI interview tool makes the stakes of profiling and automated decisions immediate.
  • A rule people can carry. "Two or more triggers" turns an official guideline into a test anyone can run.

The session draws on the three pillars of my data literacy work: what data is worth (monetary), how to work with it (technical), and how to use it responsibly (ethical). This sample sits mostly in the ethical pillar.

Next: Nomad's Compass

Game concept, in development

Nomad's Compass

A scavenger-hunt card game with an augmented reality companion app, designed to help friends explore a city together in ways that are memorable, modest and meaningful.

Type
Card game + AR app
For
Students and budget-conscious groups
Platforms
iOS and Android
Stage
Early concept

The concept

While studying in London, I started writing scavenger hunts for friends and family: riddles, clues and questions that turned seeing the city into something we solved together, for very little money. Nomad's Compass turns that habit into a game.

It takes its name from the Polynesian Wayfinders, navigators who crossed oceans by reading stars, swells and birds. The game is about that same blend of wandering and guidance.

The three guides

Tap a card to turn it over.

How it works

The box holds a deck of cards, compass on the back and a symbol on the front, plus a QR code for the free app.

  1. 1
    One player downloads the app and shuffles the deck.
  2. 2
    The group picks a theme, which shapes the whole journey:
    • Local Discovery Challenge
    • Budget Explorer Mode
    • Spin the Map Adventure
    • Night Owl Wanderer
  3. 3
    Each player draws a card showing one of the three guides.
  4. 4
    Scanning the card brings the guide to life in 3D. It introduces itself and sets a clue: a riddle, a crossword or a Jeopardy-style question.
  5. 5
    Solving the clue reveals the next destination, and the journey continues.

Why it matters to me

As a student living with real financial constraints, I wanted a way to make experiences with friends feel special without spending much. Nomad's Compass asks players to think creatively and explore wherever they are, so even a simple trip becomes an adventure.

Where it is now

Nomad's Compass is an early-stage concept that I'm now developing. I first set out the idea in an essay for the 1st Formations Business Essay.

Next: Writing

MA dissertation, University of Westminster, 2025

Can You See Me? Invisible in the Algorithm

An autoethnography and algorithmic audit of hair industry ad targeting on Instagram.

Programme
MA AI, Data & Communication
Method
Mixed methods
Platform
Instagram
Market
UK haircare

Research question

To what extent are marginalised consumers excluded from AI ad targeting in the UK haircare market?

Abstract

As AI-driven advertising disrupts the cosmetics industry, concerns about brand safety have emerged. Additionally, questions regarding the representation of marginalised consumers in digital marketing systems have raised further issues. This project investigates the ethical implications of AI ad targeting in the UK haircare market, asking: to what extent are marginalised consumers excluded from AI ad targeting in the UK haircare market?

Employing a mixed-methods design, this study combines autoethnography with an algorithmic audit of Instagram advertising. Two consumer profiles were created to observe differential ad delivery and targeting behaviour.

Findings suggest that marginalised consumers, specifically black women with afro-textured hair, are not entirely excluded from AI ad targeting but are conditionally included. Visibility depends on explicit self-identification through search terms, while neutrally coded profiles receive broader, more balanced exposure. This indicates that exclusion operates less through outright invisibility and more through undervaluation and semantic gatekeeping.

These results highlight the paradox between Black women's significant economic contributions to the haircare industry and their undervaluation in digital targeting systems. The study concludes that ethical personalisation and structural audits are essential to prevent AI-driven systems from reproducing historic hierarchies. Future research should continue to examine consumer-led interventions and the impact of regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act.

Key ideas

  • Conditional inclusion
  • Semantic gatekeeping
  • Undervaluation
  • Algorithmic auditing
  • Autoethnography
  • EU AI Act

The work connects directly to my earlier career: having managed audience targeting from the inside, I turned the same tools on a market I'm part of as a consumer.
